para_before: This study aimed to place a structured exercise program during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for stage II or III TNBC on the same cost-effectiveness scale as pembrolizumab, from the perspective of the Japanese public healthcare payer. It compared the four strategies formed by chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab and with or without exercise; it asked how large an effect on recurrence exercise would need to match pembrolizumab, in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and in net benefit; and, as its main aim, it estimated the maximum cost per patient at which exercise added to chemotherapy with pembrolizumab would be cost-effective, and how this cost depends on the size and duration of the effect of exercise on recurrence. Expressing the value of an unproven program as the cost a health system can afford for each possible effect gives future trials a benchmark for their results.

para_before: Exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy improves fitness [10–12], and supervised exercise has been delivered during neoadjuvant chemotherapy [16,17], so clinicians can offer it while its effect on recurrence is tested. Trials should record recurrence and follow patients long enough to see whether the effect lasts after the program ends; a higher pCR alone cannot settle the question. Funders can weigh the cost of such trials against the one-year net benefit if an effect is confirmed (Table S9). For payers, the price of a supervised program is far below what a confirmed effect would justify. In Japan, the fee schedule pays for rehabilitation of patients with cancer only during hospital admission, so structured exercise during outpatient neoadjuvant chemotherapy currently has no route to reimbursement [48]. Support that keeps patients exercising after surgery, such as remote programs, would add value if it extends the effect (Table S8). For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation of its perioperative indication.
